together with the commentary composed by Rājānaka Śrī Kṣemarāja.
Nourishing the gods with the spreading of his nectar, and having properly moistened the moon with his own rays, he who eternally causes the supreme essence to be tasted; and who,
when it has waned again and again, fills it once more— such is he.
I bow to the one Sun of Consciousness, whose heart exults in the divine play of the swing.
With our intellects blossoming through the helplessness induced by this immersion,
we shall reflect for a moment upon the hymn of praise to the venerable *Sāmbapañcāśikā*.
Let this supreme nectar-essence be savored here by those who know the taste;
for the touch of the immortal clarified butter of long life leads indeed to peace through the hundred-fold path.

The illustrious Sāmba, the son of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, who is fully endowed with the tradition of thousands of great yogis— masters of the secrets of the entire great lineage of the scriptures— commences the recitation of a hymn to his own self, the Sun, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world:
The Udgītha has arisen before the Lord of Rays (the Sun), whose splendor is the supreme light manifesting as the meaning of words; it precedes the circle of the three Vedas,
which dispels the darkness through the sequence of future syllables and words, by means of the seven musical notes that serve as its horses.
Salutations to that Supreme Brahman, who seems to be raising up the chariot of the two-fold knowledge. || 1 ||
Salutation to that Supreme One, the most excellent, the creator of the universe, its fullness, and so forth;

to Brahman, the Great One, the all-pervasive and the nourisher, who encompasses all forms of Brahman—such as the unmanifest (abhāva), the tranquil (śānta), the variegated (citra), and others; salutation to the conscious Self (cidātman), the creator of the universe.

The meaning is: "By means of the pacification of the state of being a subject (pramātṛtā) consisting of the body and so forth, I enter into that very [Brahman]. That Brahman, whose connection with the *udgītha*—the sound of the *praṇava*, which is the nature of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) and the first unfolding (*unmeṣa*)—is such that it is sung of or contemplated as being supreme (*utkṛṣṭatayā*) because it is non-different from the entire universe in its upward direction (*ūrdhva*). This is the *dhvani*.

The triad consisting of the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, and Yajurveda— whose primary function is the praise of the deities— is itself the "maṇḍala" (circle), by virtue of its pervasion through syntactic unity with all the scriptural utterances encompassed within the expansion [of the Vedas].
And therefore, this [is the basis] for all branches of knowledge and the specialized understandings of the mantra scriptures.

First, the sun rose, glowing intensely with its ruddy hue; it appeared as if it were itself emerging, uplifting, exalting, and— as it were— rendering everything before it identical with itself, while elevating the sky to the state of being a vehicle, a foundation, a cause of production, and the locus of action for the supreme ether.

Although this [universe] consists of space (*viyanmaya*), it is said to be "as if rising" because of its such-like manifestation, preceded by the support of the unfolding of its radiance. And this triad of spheres is [illuminated] by the radiant ones with the redness of the *prodgītha*.

That by which the darkness of ignorance is destroyed—[darkness] characterized by the flashing forth of sequences of phonemes and words, and by the succession of syllables and their denotations; that is to say, it grants repose in non-difference from the Supreme Consciousness during the utterance [of sounds], the comprehension of word-meanings, and the realization of sentence-meanings. By what? By "lifting up the sky" (viyad-unnayan). [This refers to] the seven musical notes (svaras) themselves.
The phonemes (*varṇas*), which are radiant, projectors of the universe, and animated by the primordial impulse of manifestation, are themselves the horses because they move swiftly everywhere;

these are the reflective awarenesses (*vimarśas*) of sounds such as *ṣaḍja* and so forth. Of what kind of Brahman? Of the Lord of Cows (*gopati*), the Sovereign of Speech beginning with the *parā* level, and the Lord of the Wheel of Rays (*marīcicakreśvara*). Precisely for this reason:

That supreme light, which is the Śākta vitality (*vīrya*), exists as the manifestation of this manifold variety through its own sovereignty—manifesting as the diversity of worldly and non-worldly words, their meanings, and the relations between them; and it is by that [vitality] that its radiance (*rug-dīpti*) is produced. Even in the case of the external sun, its supreme power is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).

According to the scriptural tradition that "this one indeed shines with the form of the sun," the dawn-red light, which is like a reflection of the Supreme Brahman and pervades the *praṇava*, has first arisen; [it manifests] as the orb pervading the three Vedas and the chariot pervading the other branches of knowledge, through the solar-colored syllables of ritual action.

He lifts up the sky with those horses that dispel darkness through their rhythmic strides and the placement of their feet, which pervade the seven musical notes; furthermore, this is the *udgītha*— the unfolding of the sprout of power— of the Lord of the Wheel of Consciousness (*ciccakreśvara*), whose activity consists of the world in the form of diverse signifieds and signifiers.
The blazing sphere of the triad beginning with the cosmic egg of Māyā— the root of Brahman, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—

is all-pervasive like space. It is the flow of knowledge known as Unmanā-śakti, as defined in the Vedas, which brings about the realization of the Supreme Self within the nature of beginningless consciousness.

Having first arisen as if raising up [the world] by means of various tones, mantras, and sounds, what did he do? He sequentially and in due order uttered the darkness extending up to the *samanā* level, consisting of radiant phonemes (*varṇa*), vowel-matrices (*mātrā*) beginning with *ā*, words (*pada*), and their terminations such as the *bindu*.
Wherein there is a net of snares. || 1 ||

Having thus praised the Supreme Sun by means of general pervasion, he now praises it by means of its pervasion of the central channel located within the body: "Om! That sound which constantly resounds within every living being..."

I take refuge immediately in that primordial Supreme Sun who abides within the body, from whom speech issues forth containing the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), and who carries the prāṇa and apāna breaths equally when they are mutually engaged in devouring one another.

I immediately attain—that is, I enter through focused meditative absorption—that Supreme Sun, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman, who resides within the body, established in the *prāṇa*-Brahman located in the central channel (*madhyamā nāḍī*), the primordial foundation for the canvas of the universe's manifold diversity. To the question "Which one?", he says: "That which is the syllable *oṃ*."

The Great Praṇava, whose nature is the resonance (*āda*) that embraces all sounds, resounds incessantly within every living being and all elements with an uninterrupted flow. It remains contemplating its own essential form as the Supreme Speech (*parāvāk*). And because it contains the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) within itself, its sequential unfolding is already sown therein.
The supreme, non-dual Speech, consisting of light and undivided from the mere universality of sounds from *a* to *kṣa*,
unfolds and manifests as Paśyantī; and she sustains the Prāṇa and Apāna, which are equal, having ascended to the same plane, and are intent on devouring one another, each eager to swallow the other.
He makes [them] consist of the great light of his own nature, which is the fire that carries forth the exalted breath. || 2 ||

Having thus praised the sun of consciousness (*cidarka*), which is situated in the central abode and is uninterrupted through both great pervasion (*mahāvyāpti*) and subtle pervasion (*sūkṣmavyāpti*), he now praises it also by means of its pervasion of the manifest world (*prapañcavyāpti*):
"He who [is] skin, eye, ear, tongue, nose, hand, foot, and speech..."

I take refuge in that one Sun, the twelve-fold self, who is the support of all the senses, whose form consists of mind, intellect, and ego, who abides even within the anus and the generative organ, and who illumines the world both internally and externally. (3)

This Mārtaṇḍa, the solar light of consciousness, is the animator of the "eggs"— the aggregates of body, vital breath, and so forth— which, being like corpses because they consist solely of the nature of the knowable, are devoid of life; and though he is one and without a second, he [pervades] all through his extension throughout the phenomenal world.
I take refuge in the undivided support and vitalizing substratum of the knowers, their thirteen instruments (the ten organs and the three internal faculties).
He who has assumed the form of the thirteen sense-faculties, beginning with the skin and ending with the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).

Therefore, the meaning for those of gross vision is this: the Self, which is the inner ego, exists as the subject that grasps the Vedas; externally, it remains illuminating the world—which is the object of perception—consisting of the twelvefold instruments such as the intellect and so forth, through functions like determination (adhyavasāya). But according to the secret vision:

Although he has assumed the form of all the sense organs, that single Sun of Consciousness— the twelve-fold self through his skill in the variegated movement of the circle of rays beginning with creation— is both within and without the entire universe, from the cosmic fire of time up to the subtlest digit of space.
I take refuge with excellence in Him who, illuminating the fourth state (turya) by His own innate light, causes all the organs to become a wheel;

He remains established there, having taken hold of them as their support, blazing with the splendor of His own vital energy. The meaning is: I remain, directly realizing my own emergence from that state. || 3 ||

Although the Lord— who is the support of all the senses through the pervasion of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*)— has been praised as the ultimate reality of light and awareness (*prakāśa-vimarśa*), [the author] now praises Speech (*vāṇī*), which is the path for the flow of that awareness:
"She who, emerging from the abode of Mitra and Varuṇa, [utters] the sixty-three..."

I take refuge in that Speech which first arises as Paśyantī through the manifestation of phonemes born from union with the vital breath (prāṇa), then becomes Madhyamā abiding in the intellect, and finally Vaikharī made clear by the organs of speech in the mouth. 4.

First, one should take up that [consciousness] which has arisen and blossomed at the beginning, characterized by such passages as: "But because it is undivided, Paśyantī is everywhere withdrawn from succession; it is the light of its own nature within, the subtle, imperishable speech. This [consciousness] consists of the light of its own essential nature.
Following that, one perceives that very same [speech] as established in the intellect (*buddhi*) and having attained the practice of the intellect;

solely by taking the intellect as its substrate, transcending the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), the *madhyamā* speech proceeds, following the form of sequential order—thus characterized. It is called *madhyamā* because it exists in the middle.

Next, it exists within the internal organ (the mind); thereafter, it becomes clear and stainless in the mouth—the organ of speech—specifically at the places such as the root of the tongue, the middle of the tongue, and so forth. At these locations, when the vital air (vāyu) is expanded, it assumes the form of articulated phonemes (varṇa). This is Vaikharī speech, which depends upon the activity of the breath (prāṇavṛtti) of those who employ it.
[He has] been characterized by such [passages as] these. Having entered that speech which is so named because it exists within the *vikhara* (the body), he asks: "Which one is that?
He says: "That which [proceeds] from the seat of Mitra and Varuṇa, whose nature consists of Agni and Soma."
Emerging from the supreme speech (*parāvāk*), the primary source, she utters the sixty-three phonemes (*varṇa*)—beginning with *a*—from the intermediate abode (*madhyadhāman*).

She reflects upon them through the states of difference and non-difference, as well as through difference alone, by virtue of their being strung together in a sequential order. By what means does she utter them?
By means of the instruments (*karaṇa*) which have attained the singular middle state (*madhyamā*)—an undivided and manifest luminosity—through an inward-turned orientation that is clearly evident.

By all the senses. Of what kind are these phonemes? They are those produced and manifested through contact with the vital breath (*prāṇa*). In that regard, they arise from contact with the subtle vital breath subordinated within the light of consciousness (*cij-jyotis*) in the *paśyantī* stage, and from contact with the subtle vital breath subordinated by consciousness in the *madhyamā* stage.
Due to the connection with the gross vital breath (*sthūlaprāṇa*), phonemes (*varṇa*) arise in the *vaikharī* stage of speech. These number sixty-three.
They are as follows: the four vowels *a*, *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* have twelve varieties through the distinctions of short, long, and protracted;
the vowel *ḷ* has no long form, thus it is of two kinds through the distinctions of short and protracted; and among the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), there are no short forms.

There are eight types [of vowels] due to the distinction between long and protracted. Thus, there are twenty-two vowels. There are twenty-five *sparśas* (stops) beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*. There are four *antasthās* (semivowels). There are four *ūṣmans* (sibilants). There are four *yamas* (nasalized stops), namely *kuṃ*, *khuṃ*, *guṃ*, and *dhuṃ*.

The anusvāra, visarga, jihvāmūlīya, and upadhmānīya, along with *aṃ* and *aḥ*, *ka*, and *pa*—these are the four [additional consonants]. As it has been stated: "There are twenty-two vowels, twenty-five stops (*sparśa*), eight beginning with *ya* and eight beginning with *śa*, and four *yamas* are traditionally taught."
"The anusvāra and the visarga, as well as *ka* and *pa*, are dependent on others.
These sixty-three phonemes have been declared here by the wise.
Mitra is the Sun; because he causes the burning away of all remaining duality, he is Agni. Varuṇa...

She is Soma because she bestows refreshment and nourishment. In an alternative reading, it says: "She brings forth the letters through the manifesting organs by means of their union with the vital breath. She is the power of Parāvāk, who, emerging from the abode of Mitra and Varuṇa, flows upward from the space of the Self (Ātmākāśa) by relying upon the Sun and Moon, which consist of the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge.

The stream of consciousness exists as one's own innate abode, transcending all things, and taking the form of the subject (*pramātṛ*). It is this very [stream] that, by means of the senses—which are manifest within and clearly present inside—produces or generates the sixty-three phonemes due to their conjunction with the vital breath (*prāṇa*); such is the grammatical connection. Since the senses are to be inferred from the perception of forms and other objects, they are not external.

Due to the absence of manifestness [externally], there is a manifestation within. In this context of the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the relationship between the restatement (*anuvādya*) and the injunction (*vidheya*) pertains respectively to utterance and production. || 4 ||
Having thus praised the Blessed One with the full extent of his speech, he now prays for the fruitfulness of the central abode:
"The worlds of other bodies situated above and below are arranged within [it]."
Dense with the proliferation of various channels, she dwells within all beings;
may that White One, who is the form of the Supreme Sun, be gracious to us— that Brahman-channel which is reached by those devoted to swallowing the prāṇa and apāna breaths.

May that divine form of the supreme Āditya, the sun of consciousness—which is the nature of the *brahmanāḍī*—which is lofty in appearance, gracious, praiseworthy, and which has stilled the impurities of the vital breaths and so forth, and which, for that very reason, shines as white due to its density of consciousness and bliss, remain before us. Of what nature is it? That which [extends] upwards and downwards...
The various worlds, beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Kālāgni— vast, not small, and established both externally and internally within the body, situated in the middle, and pervasively present—
likewise [reside] in the various channels (nāḍīs).

It is dense with the expansion of the cavities, from the eyes and other sense organs to the pores of the skin, and is thus difficult for all to reach; it dwells within all beings, from the immobile to the various classes of divine beings, existing in the midst of the body. And because it is dense according to the reasoning already stated, for that very reason—
Only by some, who are intent on swallowing and bold in devouring the inhalation and exhalation— the universal outflow and entry— is [the state] attained and entered. || 5 ||
Furthermore—
[the path] is not obstructed by the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), nor is it characterized by excessive cold or heat,
nor is it subject to the suffering of day and night or the affliction of the sun's heat.
May that white form of the Supreme Sun, situated within his orb and shining like the body of Vaikuṇṭha, be gracious toward us.
The cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) belongs to Brahmā, who is situated within the enclosure of the *brahmabila*;

it is an egg that contains within its womb the power (*śakti*) for the expansion of the cosmic egg of *māyā*, which has the earth as its root. The path of her [the Goddess] is such that it does not merely pass through this egg without being obstructed, but rather encompasses it on all sides; thus she is the path of expansion. Likewise, Soma is exceedingly cool.

Fire is exceedingly hot, but this [Goddess] is not of such a nature, because she burns away duality and flows with the bliss of non-duality (*advaita*); rather, her essence consists of Agni and Soma in a state of *samarasībhāva* (flavorful union). Likewise, she is "not gone" (*na-itā*) by day and night—that is, by the movement or wandering of day and night—meaning she has not fallen into the state of being an object of cognition (*prameya*). Furthermore, she is "not to be scorched" (*atāpanīyā*).

She bestows supreme bliss. Likewise, she is that from whom Rāhu—the primary obscuring factor, the void-measurer (śūnyapramātṛ)—has departed. Furthermore, she shines and blazes within the orb, the circle of rays, of the Sun, the light of consciousness. By contrast, the external form of the sun is veiled by the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and illuminates only as far as the heavenly world (svarloka).

The figure of contrast (*vyatirekadhvani*) is suggested by the fact that [this city] wanders day and night in forms of extreme cold and heat during the winter and summer seasons, causing distress, and being eclipsed by Rāhu; whereas the other is like the form of Viṣṇu (Vaikuṇṭha). Furthermore, even that [divine form], at the time of deceiving Bali, had its path obstructed within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
By someone [it is said]: "For this very reason, she is neither too cold nor too hot in nature; the meaning is that she bestows light and joy upon her devotees.

She is not measured by traveling day and night—that is, by wandering through the day and night; the meaning is that she is not limited in extent by gods and others. She is *tāpanīyā*, possessing great majesty."

"Free from Rāhu" and "having departed from the solar orb"—this is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Thus, here this *upamā-śleṣa* (simile-paronomasia) is combined with the suggestion of *vyatireka* (distinction). || 6 ||
Now he praises the form of the Sun simultaneously within and without:
"That Brahman which is mounted upon the body of the three qualities in the form of the *bindu*,
which shines as the supreme state for the lords of yogis, and which is the path to liberation— "
I have taken refuge for the sake of liberation in that which is the support of the three Vedas, the syllable Om, and the subtle sphere within the sun, yet vast even externally. || 7 ||

I have taken refuge in that orb of the fierce-rayed Sun, whose light is consciousness, for the sake of liberation—specifically for the state of liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*) attained through spiritual immersion (*samāveśa*). Of what nature is it? It is subtle within the ground of consciousness (*cidbhū*), consisting of the primordial unfolding (*unmeṣa*); it is obtainable only by the lords of yogis. And externally as well...

It is vast and of great magnitude. Within it is the *praṇava*, whose body consists of the three qualities (*guṇas*) and which is composed of the three phonemes— the short, long, and protracted vowels known as *a*, *ā*, and *aḥ*— designated as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and corresponding respectively to the qualities of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*, which effect creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
The *bindu* is the self that knows the differentiation of all that is to be known;

that which is characterized by it consists of the sequence of immeasurable states culminating in *unmanā*. Such is the Brahman—the vast and expansive—which, having ascended the splendor of *śakti*, is established in a state of supreme excellence. And that which...

It is the supreme and most extraordinary path to liberation for the lords of yogis—those who possess the singular supreme reality that transcends limited yoga—and it shines forth, manifesting through its own self-luminosity, as the means to liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). It is the foundation and support of the threefold Veda previously determined; it is praised pre-eminently, being contemplated with excellence.
Because it is that by which one attains the supreme nature of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara), it bears the name *praṇava*.
Even in the external solar orb, the body of the sun is a mandala nine thousand *yojanas* in extent;
according to the principle taught in the *Svacchanda-tantra* and other scriptures, it is threefold, wherein the form of the *bindu* is white and circular in shape.
That extraordinary image, consisting of Brahman, has ascended [to its place].
And that is the path to liberation for yogins, for it is heard that they must pierce the solar orb.
Furthermore, according to the perspective to be explained later, because it takes the form of the circles of the abodes consisting of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus, it is the support of the three Vedas.
It is called *praṇava* because it is praised pre-eminently (*prakarṣeṇa nūyamānatvāt*), and it is called *praṇava* because it has the universe as its body (*viśva-śarīratvāt*). || 7 ||
In whom the Soma, being drunk day after day by gods, ancestors, and men,
enters again and again as it is exhausted, from which it increases once more;
in whom the Vedas shine forth like honey-bees at the forefront of honey.
I take refuge in that immeasurable nectar of the sun, residing within its orb. || 8 ||

I take refuge in and resort to that immeasurable, abundant nectar of supreme bliss, which resides within the orb of the sun of consciousness (cidbhānu), situated in the central abode; wherein the moon— representing the entire range of objects of knowledge— is daily consumed by all subjects, beginning with the gods.
Because it is being drunk by means of the method of swallowing the digits (*kalā*), the moon—becoming ever more diminished—enters again and again;

having rested in the heart, it subsequently sinks. From that very mandala, the moon, which consists of the forms of objects of knowledge (*meyarūpa*), increases and becomes manifest once more. And within it reside the Vedas and all the scriptures.

In the honey of the *mākṣika* bees, the forms of the *saraghā* bees appear as if before one's eyes, shimmering in front; just as the *saraghā* bees, having gathered the *mākṣika* honey and turned back, sit there full of joy, so too do all the Vedas shine, having touched upon the supreme non-dual nectar through the syntactic unity of their statements.

The external moon as well, having its fifteen digits consumed by the ancestors, gods, and humans during the dark fortnights, enters the solar orb on the new moon day and increases; meanwhile, the Vedas remain established in the light of the sun and the ascendant. || 8 ||
Having filled the eastern quarter with his broad form, he gradually traversed the seven worlds with that foot by which the manifest deer-marked one (the moon) was surpassed;
having cast the darkness into the netherworld, where it dissolved and vanished from sight.
Victorious is that Sun, the light of the universe, whose rays of pure being shine upward.

According to the established principle that "he who is superior in quality to another is considered to be above him," he is one whose rays are "upward"— that is, supreme over the universe. For this very reason,
the "being" (*sattva*) of all existing things without exception is his own nature, which consists of the essence of great luminosity.

That alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Consequently, because the universe is submerged within the very self of light by virtue of its being manifest, light is the illumination of the universe; that alone, the sun of consciousness, triumphs, existing with supreme excellence, by which it [illuminates] the eastern quarter—the state of initial emergence—with its vast form.

Having filled [the universe] by means of the subtle vibration of Śakti accessible to yogis, and having caused it to surge forth through the predominance of consciousness characterized by the contraction of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so on,
those who range from Śiva down to the individual soul (sakala) are proclaimed as "possessors of power" (śaktimant), according to the rule taught in the *Śrīpūrva* and other scriptures.

The seven worlds— known as Śiva, Mantramahēśvara, Mantreśvara, Mantravijñānākala, Pralayākala, and Sakala— which reside respectively in the *tuṭi*s of the vital breath and are accompanied by their own powers, are pervaded by His "foot" according to the principle that "His foot is all beings"; having embraced them, He occupies them with His own portion alone.

They have been made to consist of His own light. Of what sort is He? He whose "haris"—the powers of the eyes and other senses—are manifest as the reflections of His own Self and are "haras" because they seize the universe of forms and so forth. As it is said in the Śruti: "For ten hundred haris are yoked to Him. The meaning of this is that the Self possesses innumerable powers. How so?
Have they crossed? Having caused the darkness—the ignorance consisting in the perception of the non-self as the self—to dissolve within themselves;

having made that which is hidden in the netherworld, characterized by the manifestation of the designation of "self" in what is not the self, entirely extinguished; and having [conquered] the eastern quarter with the external sun mounted upon seven horses—[have they crossed]?

Having filled the quarters with its subtle form, the worlds beginning with Bhūr were traversed in succession by its rays, which dispelled the darkness with their feet; and by Nārāyaṇa, manifest as Hari, that darkness— the family of Dānavas— was dissolved, wherein the manifestation of the lord of Dānavas named Bali was destroyed.

Having caused [the earth] to sink into the netherworld (pātāla), the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ were traversed by the sequence of his footsteps. Having done what? Having filled the quarters of Indra and the other directions with his broad body—that is, with the form of a dwarf child.

Furthermore, the term *viśvāloka* (the light of the universe) here contains the poetic figure of paronomasia (*śleṣa*), as it implies both "the world of all" and "one whose nature is predominantly *sattva*."
This is a combination of paronomasia, simile, and suggestion. || 9 ||
Having meditated upon the first, subtle Brahman resounding at the root of the vital breath,
and having clearly uttered the Vyāhṛtis resonant with the Praṇava within,
[one should contemplate] that which is called "Tat" in the Veda, the excellent [Brahman] spoken of by Savitṛ.
I take refuge in that indescribable, supreme abode called Bharga, which contains within it all splendors. || 10 ||

By Brahmā Prajāpati, preceded by the utterance of the syllable *oṃ*—the mouth of the *praṇava*—within the Vedas, [he taught] that which begins with "tat" and so forth; [referring to] the Gāyatrī, whose source is Savitṛ, the universal progenitor, the conscious Sun; that which is called *bhargas*, which is indescribable (*yattatkiṃapi*) and extraordinary, the supreme, most excellent.

I take refuge in—that is, I enter—that most excellent and grace-bestowing abode (dhāma), which is the radiant power of Śakti, containing within itself all other abodes such as the external sun, moon, and fire, because it encompasses them all. Having done what was said by Brahmā? [The answer follows: "I bow to that supreme Śakti, who is the primordial cause of the universe, who is the mother of the three worlds, who is the source of the Vedas, and who is the supreme Brahman. What is the nature of that abode? It is the light of Śakti whose essence is throbbing radiance, and it is the womb of all abodes because it embraces the external abodes of the sun, moon, fire, and so forth. It is most excellent and bestows grace. Having done what was said by Brahmā? [He says: "I bow to that supreme Śakti... and so on. What is the nature of that Śakti? She is the primordial cause of the universe, the mother of the three worlds, the source of the Vedas, and the supreme Brahman. What is the meaning of "I bow"? It means I prostrate myself before her with my entire body, speech, and mind. What is the nature of that Śakti? She is the primordial cause of the universe, the mother of the three worlds, the source of the Vedas, and the supreme Brahman. What is the meaning of "supreme"? It means she is beyond the reach of the senses and the mind, and she is the ultimate reality. What is the meaning of "Brahman"? It means she is the absolute reality, the source of all things, and the one without a second. What is the meaning of "source of the Vedas"? It means she is the origin of the four Vedas and the sixty-four auxiliary sciences. What is the meaning of "mother of the three worlds"? It means she is the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the three worlds. What is the meaning of "primordial cause of the universe"? It means she is the root cause of the entire cosmic manifestation. What is the meaning of "I take refuge in"? It means I surrender my self to her and seek her protection. What is the meaning of "I enter"? It means I merge my consciousness with hers and become one with her. What is the meaning of "most excellent"? It means she is the highest goal and the ultimate object of attainment. What is the meaning of "grace-bestowing"? It means she is the source of all blessings and the remover of all obstacles. What is the meaning of "light of Śakti"? It means she is the self-luminous consciousness that illumines all things. What is the meaning of "womb of all abodes"? It means she is the ground of all existence and the source of all manifestations. What is the meaning of "encompasses them all"? It means she is the totality of all things and there is nothing outside of her. What is the meaning of "radiant power of Śakti"? It means she is the dynamic energy that animates the universe. What is the meaning of "throbbing radiance"? It means she is the ever-active, pulsating consciousness that is the very life-force of the cosmos. What is the meaning of "supreme"? It means she is the transcendental reality that is beyond all limitations and categories. What is the meaning of "absolute reality"? It means she is the non-dual truth that is the final resort of all inquiry. What is the meaning of "one without a second"? It means she is the undivided whole in which no duality exists. What is the meaning of "root cause of the cosmic manifestation"? It means she is the primal seed from which the entire universe emerges. What is the meaning of "surrender my self to her"? It means I relinquish all egoistic attachments and place my total trust in her. What is the meaning of "merge my consciousness with hers"? It means I dissolve the boundaries of my individuality and experience union with the universal consciousness. What is the meaning of "become one with her"? It means I attain the state of identity with the supreme Śakti and realize my true nature as the eternal, blissful Self. What is the meaning of "highest goal"? It means she is the ultimate destination for all seekers of liberation. What is the meaning of "ultimate object of attainment"? It means she is the fruit of all spiritual practice and the end of all human endeavor. What is the meaning of "remover of all obstacles"? It means she is the compassionate protector who dispels all fears and difficulties. What is the meaning of "self-luminous consciousness"? It means she is the innate light of awareness that shines forth without depending on any external source. What is the meaning of "ground of all existence"? It means she is the substratum upon which the entire world is projected. What is the meaning of "undivided whole"? It means she is the seamless unity that transcends all distinctions and dualities. What is the meaning of "non-dual truth"? It means she is the reality that cannot be grasped by the intellect or expressed in words. What is the meaning of "final resort of all inquiry"? It means she is the conclusion reached by all philosophical investigation and the answer to all existential questions. What is the meaning of "primal seed"? It means she is the creative impulse that initiates the process of manifestation. What is the meaning of "eternal, blissful Self"? It means I am not merely a limited individual soul, but the infinite, joyful consciousness that is identical with the supreme Śakti. What is the meaning of "attain the state of identity"? It means I do not merely worship her from a distance, but I realize that I am her very self. What is the meaning of "realize my true nature"? It means I awaken to the fact that my essential being is one with the divine. What is the meaning of "infinite, joyful consciousness"? It means I am no longer bound by the constraints of time, space, or causality, but I dwell in the eternal bliss of the absolute. What is the meaning of "not merely a limited individual soul"? It means I am not a transient entity subject to birth and death, but I am the immortal witness of all phenomena. What is the meaning of "awaken to the fact"? It means I gain direct, immediate knowledge of my own divinity through the grace of the Guru and the power of meditation. What is the meaning of "direct, immediate knowledge"? It means I do not rely on indirect inference or conceptual understanding, but I experience the truth firsthand. What is the meaning of "grace of the Guru"? It means the transformative power transmitted by the realized teacher who has himself attained this state. What is the meaning of "power of meditation"? It means the focused concentration that pierces through the layers of ignorance and reveals the hidden light of the Self. What is the meaning of "pierces through the layers of ignorance"? It means it destroys the deep-seated illusions that veil our true nature. What is the meaning of "reveals the hidden light"? It means it uncovers the radiant consciousness that has always been present but was previously obscured. What is the meaning of "always been present"? It means it is the unchanging reality that persists through all states of being. What is the meaning of "previously obscured"? It means it was covered by the veils of Maya and the accumulated impressions of past actions. What is the meaning of "uncovering the radiant consciousness"? It means making manifest the self-effulgent awareness that is the core of our being. What is the meaning of "self-effulgent awareness"? It means an awareness that does not depend on the senses or the mind, but is its own source of light. What is the meaning of "core of our being"? It means it is the very essence of who we truly are, beyond the body and the mind. What is the meaning of "beyond the body and the mind"? It means it is the witness-consciousness that observes the activities of both without being affected by them. What is the meaning of "witness-consciousness"? It means the pure subjectivity that remains constant even when the objects of perception change. What is the meaning of "pure subjectivity"? It means the fundamental "I-ness" that is free from all objective attributes and limitations. What is the meaning of "fundamental 'I-ness'"? It means the primordial sense of self-existence that precedes all notions of "this" or "that. What is the meaning of "free from all objective attributes"? It means it is devoid of qualities such as form, color, size, or number. What is the meaning of "free from all limitations"? It means it is not confined by time, space, or causality. What is the meaning of "not confined by time, space, or causality"? It means it is the timeless, spaceless, and causeless reality that is the ground of all existence. What is the meaning of "timeless, spaceless, and causeless reality"? It means it is the absolute truth that is beyond all relative categories and definitions. What is the meaning of "ground of all existence"? It means it is the substratum upon which the entire universe is supported. What is the meaning of "entire universe"? It means the totality of all names and forms, including the gods, humans, animals, and inanimate objects. What is the meaning of "supported"? It means it is held together by the power of that single reality and would collapse without it. What is the meaning of "single reality"? And having done what, shall I take refuge? First, at the outset, [I take refuge] in the bodiless (*atanu*),

the supreme Śākta abode (*dhāma*) known as Vīreśvara— which is the Great (*bṛhat*) and Expansive (*bṛṃhaka*) Brahman, consisting of the reflective awareness of the letter *A* according to the method taught in the *Śrībhargaśikhā* and other scriptures— located at the root of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Having meditated upon and reflected within the abode where breath and the like do not manifest, one sees— that is, realizes as one's own self— the one called *nāda*, which resounds immediately thereafter; it is the essence of supreme awareness (*paravimarśa*), existing as the internalized state of vitality through the aforementioned nature of Śakti.

Preceded by the utterance of the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) which unfolds through the power of the firm support of entering into the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that resonance (*nāda*), there is likewise the form of the mantra:
*bhūḥ svāhā*, *bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *svaḥ svāhā*, and *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā*.

This [mantra] pertains to the entire range of the objects of knowledge (*meyas*), the means of knowledge (*mānas*), and the subjects of knowledge (*pramātṛs*), together with their latent impressions (*saṃskāras*).

Having correctly uttered the four *vyāhṛtis* while maintaining the internal awareness of their being composed of the Supreme Brahman— without any slackening of the support provided by that inner realization— and furthermore,
according to the method taught in the *Śivasūtras* and other texts, [performing] "japa" as the discourse of all worldly activities in their manifold forms; |||

The meaning is: having rendered [all things] saturated with the essence of the supreme Śakti by making the primary focus the contemplation of their non-difference from that [Śakti]; and then, by the power of taking hold of the abode of Śambhu—which is attained through the force of one-pointed concentration on the abode of Śakti—having made even the state of worldly emergence (vyutthāna) sprinkled with the essence of non-difference from that [Śakti].
In the phrase "dhāmagarbham," the word *dhāma* is repeated by way of *tantra*; likewise, [it is applied] in the phrase "praṇavamukharam."

O Blessed One, the notion that "I shall praise you with hymns"— this grasping at duality consisting of the praiser, the praised, and the act of praising— is itself ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the non-manifestation of non-dual consciousness (*cidadvaya*). Nevertheless, for the complete destruction and total uprooting of that very ignorance, it is fitting [for me] to be ever-connected to you.
