He is of the singular nature of self-luminous consciousness, yet not limited by space; for even the subtle atom is an object of cognition and is visible. He is most vast and all-pervading. And thus, because He encompasses the universe, He has the form of the universe. Because He is endowed with qualities such as omniscience, He possesses attributes (saguṇa). Thus it is said.

By this expression— referring to that which has limbs (aṅga) consisting of various distinct parts (avayavabhāga) in the form of specific attributes (tattaddharmarūpa), each separately delineated by a particular mode of conceptualization (kalpanā)—
it is shown that [the ultimate reality] is the one supreme [principle], untouched by verbal conceptualizations whose objects are delimited entities.
He suggests that its own nature (*svarūpa*) is unconditioned. "Diverse" refers to the various living beings, from stationary objects up to the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*);

their "primordial natures" (*prakṛti*) are the causes such as *māyā-prakṛti*, semen, and blood; and their "transformations" (*vikṛti*) are the [evolutes] such as the *kalās*, the intellect (*buddhi*), and the body.
The meaning is: he who shines while manifesting [all things], or he who throbs by virtue of causing the emergence of all contracted manifestations.
In the exposition of reality, the sages, speaking "not this, not this," became exhausted; they did not say "you are exactly that," nor did they say "you are such-and-such.
Therefore, I utter to you only these words: "Salutation to You."
For, generally speaking, the speech of this [work], which is pregnant with knowledge, spreads forth most extensively. || 13 ||

Since from you the speech of Bhārati—consisting of Paśyantī and the other levels, pregnant with knowledge, and primarily characterized by self-luminous consciousness—emanates, to you I offer only this much: "Salutation," and no further words of praise or the like. For [you are] the undivided cause of the emanation of all speech, which is itself knowledge.

This is because you cannot be praised by words of diverse hymns; however, it is possible to perform an act of prostration—of the body and so forth—and to reflect upon the excellence of your own fourth state of pure consciousness by means of the word "namaḥ. And this is appropriate, because even the sages, regarding you as the subject of the declaration of reality, [perceive you] as neither minute nor great, nor short.

Those who say "it is not long," and so forth, are exhausted and afflicted; yet they have not correctly described You as being such-and-such, or of this kind, or equal to that, because You are simply beyond the range of speech. This is the meaning. || 13 ||
You, who are the inner self (antarātman) dwelling within the interior of all bodies, pervading every limb,
are not perceived by those devoid of reasoning, just as fire is not seen within wood [by the unskilled]. And you, who are churned from the fire-drills of the vital breaths by the steadfast ones—
O Supreme Āditya, you become the visible light; salutations to you! || 14 ||

O Supreme Sun, O Conscious Light, salutations to You, the Indifferentiated One! You are Bhava, the pervasive one, who exists within all limbs of all Rudras and individual souls (kṣetrajñas), from the immobile beings up to the divine classes; You are the Inner Self (antarātmā) within the limited perceiving self, which is Your own essential nature.
Because you are supreme bliss, you are both the Self and the Inner Self; thus,

though you abide as the subject of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*) as taught in the *Śrī Svacchanda* and other scriptures, and though you remain present even while not dwelling in any particular state, you are not perceived even by those who are empty [of realization], despite your presence through logic and yoga— just as fire remains within wood.
It is not seen by those devoid of reasoning who are ignorant of the friction-stick (araṇi);

it is not perceived as having the nature of a blazing flame within the mouthful of wood. And you, [O Lord], are present in the life-force-friction-sticks—the resting places where all paths of the breath arise.

When [the centers] are being churned by virtuous yogins who are self-controlled and diligent— through the descent of the upward power and the contraction of the downward power— he who understands the penetration of Rudra’s power is a wise man.
Thus, through the continuous oscillation prescribed by the traditional scriptures and logical reasoning, you become the visible light that pervades the breath once it has been stilled;

you shine forth as the self-luminous form of consciousness. In this process, the prāṇa and apāna breaths serve respectively as the upper and lower kindling woods, while the effort of the yogi is the friction-stick. 14.

The praiser, the object of praise, and the act of praise—you alone, whose nature consists of agent, action, and object, sport in this performance of your own glorification; therefore, I am not independent in this matter.
Or rather, O Lord of the Cowherds, that which I speak, made beautiful by my affection, is indeed the truth.
For what else indeed could exist in the worlds apart from you? That [which is otherwise] would be false. || 15 ||

O Gopati, O Lord of the wheel of pure rays, you alone are without a second; through your own sovereignty, you sport in the form of hymns and the like, manifesting as those various forms. As I have stated in my *Bhairavānukaraṇastotra*: "The worshipper, the object of worship, and the worship—even though these appear distinct..."
"Whatever exists here, in whatever form you perceive it, that becomes [manifest] as the nature of consciousness.

Since "I" is merely imagined by you, therefore, as the limited subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) characterized primarily by contraction, I am dependent in composing this hymn to you; I praise you alone, who are the self of consciousness, for I am not some other entity called "I."

The meaning is "someone. And whatever I, who am identical with you, the Self, say—charming through affection and beautiful in its supplication—all that is true, for it is indeed your own ultimate reality.
Since what exists apart from you, the conscious Self, could there be anything at all in the worlds? There is nothing whatsoever. Or rather:

Nevertheless, if anything were to be conceptualized, that would be false; it could not exist at all. Since there can be no consciousness whatsoever apart from the nature of Consciousness (cidātmatā), even the status of being an object of thought and conceptualization is impossible for it, making it more insubstantial than a flower in the sky. Thus, by way of reasoning, this praise has as its very essence non-difference from You. || 15 ||
Although there is indeed a distinction according to the conventional sequence of perception, he says that you are nevertheless to be worshipped by us in this way:
"Knowledge does not exist for people like us without the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)."
And you are utterly inconceivable because you are beyond the range of all the senses;
since you are beyond meditation, you cannot be attained except through the yoga of devotion.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining immortality, I have taken refuge in devotion. || 16 ||
For us, who are illusory subjects possessing sensory cognition, you— who are beyond the range of the senses—
do not become an object of meditation because of your inconceivability; therefore,
[this is] the yoga of devotion consisting in the worship of the sun of consciousness, which involves the immersion and emergence from the limited subjectivity of the body and so forth.

Because it is that which must be accomplished, I have taken refuge in devotion alone to the Blessed One for the sake of attaining the nectar consisting of the intense immersion (*sphāra-āveśa*) of power (*śākta*). And it is said in the *Vijñānabhairava*:
"The state that arises in one who is detached through the excess of devotion—that is the Power of Śaṅkara."
Then Śiva should constantly meditate upon her. Thus [ends verse 16].
Arising first, she destroys the darkness residing in the hearts of those who have taken refuge in it;

thereafter, through the sequence of the application of action and the predominance of *sattva*, she destroys *rajas*; and when well-practiced, having reached its culmination, she causes *sattva* alone to expand further.
O Sun, for those who have attained tranquility, you lead them toward Nirvana, just as the three Vedas lead the disciplined.

O Arka, your devotion, having been attained and taking refuge [in you], leads to the liberation (nirvāṇa) of those who are tranquil—that is, those whose stains such as passion have been stilled—and it serves to manifest the state of being Śiva while yet alive. It is just like the Three Vedas (trayī); for even that [Vedic path] consists of ritual actions performed with desire.

When practiced after having abandoned [worldly desires], it is the cause of liberation for those who know the end of the three Vedas. Thus, this [knowledge], when first proclaimed, destroys the *āṇava* impurity— which consists of the non-discriminatory ignorance (*abhedākhyāti*) of the darkness residing in the heart— among the devotees who have merely begun to awaken the light and bliss of the Self within their hearts.

It destroys [the impurity]. Thereafter, through the excellence and intensity of *sattva*—that is, light (*prakāśa*)—and by means of the sequence of the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), namely the performance of bodily rites whose fruit is repose in one’s own self as the deity, it destroys *rajas*, which consists of the impurity of action (*kārmamala*). Likewise, *sattva* is that state of being (*bhāva*) which is well-practiced and mastered through constant cultivation.

The very state of being a single mass of light manifests even more intensely everywhere within that which is shining; it does not, like the bound soul (paśu), produce the manifestation of objects as distinct from itself due to the impurity of māyā. Even the three Vedas manifest that reality for those who know the end of the three and are established therein. 17.
Having obtained her— who is like prosperity in one's home, like a wish-fulfilling cow during travel,
like radiance in darkness, like fortitude in the forest, and like the Brahma-nāḍī for a league—
she is a boat in this ocean of saṃsāra, which is filled with crocodiles in the form of treacherous sense objects.
May I go to that supreme nectar of yours which is neither cold nor hot. || 18 ||
Relying upon that devotion, may I go to—that is, enter—the supreme, immortal, and transcendent abode of Śakti belonging to you, the Sun of Consciousness;
which, because it is distinct from the external solar light of the winter and summer solstices, is neither cold nor hot. Moreover...

It is of the nature of fire and moon, producing delusion, burning, illumination, and joy. Of what sort is it? It is like Fortune (Śrī) in an empty house—that is, in a vacant dwelling—because it bestows all enjoyments in their fullness; it is like the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) in a place where one's kinsmen are absent during travel, because it grants the desired fruits of one's thoughts merely by being contemplated; and it is like [light] in the darkness of dense gloom.

It shines as it were, because it is the cause of full manifestation. It is like a support in the forest, in dense jungles, on mountains, and so forth, because it is the cause of rest. It is the *brahmanāḍī*, the *suṣumnā*, within the *yojana*—the immersion into identity with the Supreme Śiva—because it is the supreme means (*upāya*). It is such that its terrifying aquatic predators are the very objects of sense-perception, which are difficult to traverse.
It is like a boat in the ocean of saṃsāra, because it brings one across. || 18 ||
O Blessed One, Agni and Soma are the cause of the entire world; at the beginning of creation, You emit them through Your rays according to the sequence of waning and waxing.
Those very two, made equal within the fire of the Self by those who offer oblations during the equinox, [attain their true nature].
You cause both of these to set simultaneously for the sake of the liberation of those who possess devotion. || 19 ||

O Blessed One, for this entire world— comprising the external objects of perception such as blue and pleasure, and the internal perceiving forms such as the body— the cause is the prāṇa and apāna, which carry all flows and consist of fire (nī) and moon (so),
because they are the causes of manifestation and stability respectively. These two...

At the time of the withdrawal, entry, and taking up of the self-emanation— namely, at the beginning of the creation consisting of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that manifests as objects— the [Lord] performs creation and so forth by means of rays, through the sequence of decrease and increase,
according to the successive cycles of the twelve and sixteen digits (*kalās*), for the sake of that [emanation].
O Goddess, you repeatedly create and fashion [the world] with the rays of your own self; and those very two,

when properly directed within the equinox of the devotees— during the *kumbhaka* breath-retention where the vital winds are perfectly balanced and the digits of the moon and sun are blended through mutual friction— are equalized.

For those offering oblations into the fire of their own self and the fire of *udāna* for the sake of liberation— so that they may attain the non-duality of Śiva, characterized by the burning away of the three impurities such as *āṇava* which consist of the manifestation of the distinction between Śiva and the self— you, with your very rays, simultaneously bring both of these to their end through the process of sequential stages.

Having entered into the pervasion of the vyāna breath, which is the soul of the universe, you bring about your own self as consisting of the supreme fire and moon, whose nature is knowledge and action. || 19 ||

Your grossness is unfathomable by nature and cannot be perceived, for you are infinite; likewise, your subtlety is inconceivable because of the absence of any manifestation as either being or non-being.
Thus I meditate—how can I know You, who are without beginning or end?
Therefore, O Sun, be gracious to me, your devotee, by your own self.

O Arka (Sun), your grossness—your pervasiveness throughout the universe—cannot be perceived at all because of its inherent profundity; for it is infinite, being unconditioned by the dimensions of space, time, and form.
Or rather, your subtlety is such that you are "smaller than the smallest," according to the reasoning explained on the occasion of commenting upon that very phrase.

That which consists of the nature of the supreme subject is also inconceivable, because it is not perceived as having the form of existence or non-existence due to the absence of the manifestation of being or non-being.
Thus, since You are without beginning or end and remain unknown, how can I contemplate You within my own heart?
Somehow! Therefore, since I am devoted to you and attentive to your prayer, be gracious of your own accord;
with the turbidity of the conceit of being a limited subject regarding the body and so forth stilled, shine forth! 20.
That ineffable, supreme essence of sound which is to be known— you, dwelling within, desiring to manifest as that Reality, slowly take up the measures and portions in the ether;
arising from the *bindu* and *nāda*, you do so through the unmanifest form of the *praṇava*.
Or, for you, the denoter is that which is manifested by the organs through the utterance of the Word-Brahman. || 21 ||
Whatever is extraordinary,

that you [should place] within that state which consists of the inward-turned, undivided Light; for the scripture declares that "the reality of sound (śabdatattva) is everything whose nature is sound," and it is proclaimed that "sound is the *haṃsa*."
The form of the Lord Anāhata-bhaṭṭāraka, as taught in the *Śrī-svacchanda* and other scriptures, is "supreme" (*paramam*), meaning most excellent.

As it is stated in the *Śrī-kālottara*: "That which is called Nāda is the supreme seed. It is "to be known" (*vedyam*) because its nature is one of perfectly manifest and radiant luminosity, and thus it is not subject to denial; however, it is not something that constitutes the object of the act of knowing.
As it is said in the *Śrīsvacchanda*: "How can he who has neither form nor body, nor color nor action— being subtle, ungraspable, eternal, and immutable— be apprehended?"
Also in the *Śrībhargaśikhā*:
"This is neither a phoneme nor a word, nor is it composed of *kalās*;
it is the absolute, supreme bliss, the hero, the eternally risen sun."
"It neither sets nor rises; it is neither quiescent nor subject to transformation.
Moving within all beings, the Sun is remembered as Bharga.
This very form possesses the power of the Supreme Brahman-Atman; it is that which desires to attain manifestation as the existent (sat). Thus: "Oṃ tat sat."

According to the established principle that "the instruction regarding Brahman is remembered as threefold," [the practitioner], desiring to grasp the nature of Brahman which consists of power (śakti) and the self (ātman),

gradually and sequentially takes up— that is, receives— the *kalās*, which are the powers of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) consisting of the *mātrās* such as *a*, *u*, and *m*, within the void of the abode of Suṣumṇā. Thus...
Upon the wall of the Śabdabrahman illuminated by the sun of conscious power (cidarka), [He resides] in the form of the unmanifest Praṇava— the essence of the syllable Oṃ—

in the form primarily of Paśyantī speech, and not in a manifest form that touches the stages of speech such as Madhyamā and the rest; for it is established that "the Praṇava is present in all the Vedas."

The Śabdabrahman, having embraced the entire expanse of the signified and the signifier, utters itself and proceeds; it is not, however, uttered by another. Of what nature is it? It has arisen from *bindu* and *nāda*, which consist respectively of the cognition that is undivided from all objects of knowledge (*vedya*) and the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that is undivided from all signifiers (*vācaka*).
How can the True Word (satkatha), which has ascended to the most supreme sky, be uttered? To this, he recalls the reasoning found in the scriptures:

it is manifested—that is, made manifest—not by means of the vocal organs (*karaṇa*) through the binding of divine instruments (*divyakaraṇabandha*), nor by the root of the tongue, the palate, and so forth. As it is said in the *Śrīsvacchanda*:
"Having made the divine instrument, perform the utterance of the reality," and so forth.

And this [mantra], by means of the reflective awareness of the very nature of the power of the reality of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahma*), is its designator and the reflector of its own nature. || 21 ||
In the morning, that which possesses the form of the sun's rays at dawn is the *rājasa* Veda; that which shines as if ablaze in the midday with white luster is the *sāttvika* Yajus;
and in the evening, that which has the rays set and takes on a form radiant with darkness is the Sāman.
Your form is like the three Vedas in the process of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the day.

O Blessed One, O Sun of Consciousness (*cidarka*), that activity of Yours which pertains to the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universal day—the day of the vital breath—is the power called the Fourth (*turyā*), which unfolds having embraced the entirety of creation and the rest; this is the meaning. To the question "Which one is that?", he says:

In the morning, at the dawn whose nature is the opening of the heart, when the functions of the prāṇa and apāna have become subordinate, there is the twilight (saṃdhyā) consisting of the union of Śiva and Śakti; that which partakes of those crimson rays— shining because their manifold variety has not yet fully blossomed— which are the body and so forth, as well as the illuminations of the eyes and other senses, is what is meant here.
Thus, the *Ṛgveda* consists of the Rājasa principle; it is the universal sovereign (*viśvarāj*), the thread that extends throughout the universe, and is composed of the *Ṛks*.
Furthermore, its essence is the contemplation of the supreme abode, and it performs praise in the intermediate space.
The *Yajurveda*, moreover, is primarily characterized by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) consisting of the ritual worship of deities. It blazes as if to consume the fuel of duality.
The stainless self-radiance is the true nature, possessing white luster due to the emergence of the pervasive moon whose essence is refreshment.
It is the *sattva*—the state of being of the virtuous—and it brings about this [state];
that is to say, through the immersion in its own self-luminosity, it illuminates the entire universe.

In the evening, during the half-tuṭi following the [previous] one, the rays have set; because the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth have dissolved and perished, the mass of rays is both tranquil and intensely radiant. And for this reason, through the swallowing of both the impressionless duality and non-duality, and by virtue of that very [swallowing], there is a state of single flavor due to resting in the reality of darkness.

Sāman. This threefold nature—consisting of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme—which you enjoy and which you grasp, is your form, like the triple Veda: the Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman. To explain: in the morning, there is the pervasion of the Ṛgveda, primarily consisting of hymns of praise to the deity Arka; at midday, there is the emergence of the Yajurveda, consisting of the performance of ritual acts; and in the evening...
The daily practice consists primarily of songs for the sake of repose and primarily of the Sāmaveda. || 22 ||
Those who have resorted to the seven suns resounding through the mouths of the meters— the seeds of the netherworld, the ocean, the sages, the mountains, the islands, and the worlds—
and those who have mounted the single horse that is the mere state of partless speech;
They go toward you alone, who are devoid of even a fraction of the qualities of the celestial realm, without a horse.

The seven netherworlds beginning with Atala; the seven oceans beginning with the Ocean of Milk; the seven sages beginning with Atri; the seven mountains beginning with Mahendra; the seven continents beginning with Jambūdvīpa;
and the seven worlds beginning with Bhūrloka.
Delusion, intoxication, pride, despondency,
anger, fear, and joy— these are known as the seven afflictions within the body.

Thus have been stated the seven afflictions beginning with delusion (*moha*). The seven seeds are barley and so forth. The seven meters are the *gāyatrī* and so forth. They are called "beings" (*bhūta*) because they have come into existence (*prāpta*). Those who possess in their mouths the seven musical notes (*svara*), such as *ṣaḍja* and the rest, which take the form of this entire cosmic manifestation (*viśvaprapañca*), are [the ones referred to].

Having you as their mouth, they have taken refuge in you— those seven steeds consisting of mind, intellect, and the senses, which neigh and sound forth those very same meanings. And those who are partless, mounted upon the mere existence (*tanmātra*) of that state of speech known as *paśyantī*.

Having realized You as the one who is both the "Single Horse" (Ekāśva) and yet the "Horseless One" (Anaśva)—the Supreme Brahman, the Sun of Consciousness—those who have taken refuge in You, both [groups], attain You alone;

they reach oneness with You. Of what nature are You? [You are] characterized by the musical notes (*svaras*) such as *ṣaḍja* and the like, which are Your qualities (*guṇas*), and are touched by the awareness of the *paśyantī* [speech] emerging from the central channel (*madhyadhāma*).
It is devoid of the *kalās* such as *sattva* and the vowels beginning with *a*; it is a mass of unconditioned light and bliss.
That this [which is devoid of all] is the cause for attaining the eternal through non-eternal worship is an apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*). || 23 ||
Having filled the three worlds with divine light through water and wind, and having again taken up that essence with your rays,
you enter the earth hidden within; dwelling therein, you bring forth food.
And that [Self] is the vital breath; O Sustainer of the worlds, you are the Sun, the Self of all living beings. || 24 ||

O Blessed One, having filled the three worlds— the triad of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— with light, water, and wind, and with the vital breaths that are the nectar of Śakti entering the cavities that illuminate consciousness,
You have attained a divine state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya) unified within those very three worlds.

Taking up again and again the essence—the solid mass of the bliss of the Fourth—with the unsurpassed rays of light, and having experienced a state of wonder, you dissolve into the inward-facing state; thus you enter the supreme ground, the Earth, and through identification with it, you shine forth.
Having entered that, you bring forth the entire range of objects of knowledge, including food, passion, and sensory domains.

Having become solidified, you manifest in that very form; and that food is the cause for the persistence of the prāṇa and apāna, which is none other than you yourself. By this reasoning, you are called both the sun and the soul of all living beings. As the Śruti says:
"I am food, I am the giver of food, and I am the eater of food. Even the external sun,
having at various times filled the three worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar— with light, water, and wind,
becomes one in essence with the divine essence in the form of *rasa* (flavor/nectar) throughout the three worlds.

Having drawn [the essence] from the earth at the beginning of summer by means of its rays, it enters again into the earth, becoming dissolved through the process of internal heating. Having entered therein, it produces food known as herbs, which is the cause for the maintenance of the vital breaths (prāṇas).
Therefore, that very [sun] is the food, the giver of food, and the eater of food. || 24 ||

The yogi who, having internalized within himself Agni and Soma, Prakṛti and Puruṣa, Bindu and Nāda, the eternal Prāṇa and Apāna, as well as day and night, and the two— truth and falsehood, merit and demerit, existence and non-existence, and both— is [liberated].
With his mind stilled within himself, he shall abide and enter into you, who are devoid of qualities.

The yogi perceives the two ever-present and continuously flowing prāṇa and apāna as Agni and Soma because they are the causes of consumption and nourishment; as Prakṛti and Puruṣa due to the predominance of the powers of knowledge and action; as Bindu and Nāda because they consist of sensation and reflective awareness; and as Day and Night because they are the states of expansion and rest.

Having dissolved within himself—within the abode of consciousness (ciddhāman)—the pairs of existence and non-existence, truth and falsehood (which are the causes of expansion and contraction, and the causes of upward and downward movement, namely merit and demerit), as well as the external notions of being and non-being, and having merged them all into the internal abode of the vital breath (udāna), he should abide established in the Self; such a person is indeed devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). You [should become] that.
He indeed enters the Supreme Sun, which transcends the qualities of sattva and the rest. || 25 ||

Standing between the two lotus-faces of Heaven and Earth as they slept for the purpose of conception and birth, he, situated in the midst of the beloved pair, seemed to awaken them face-to-face through the light of the moon and the rays of the sun, using the clouds as his mouth.
O Blessed One, you drink even by turns, being greedy for the taste of the six flavors. || 26 ||

O Blessed One, O Sun of Consciousness! In the lotus-face of You, whose body is the intermediate space between the two beloved ones—Heaven and Earth—which have been rendered beautiful solely by Your own self-knowledge and who extend to the limit of all twelve; within that lotus of power...
Having awakened and caused [the senses] to blossom through the unsurpassed cow-faced rays,
you— being greedy for the savoring of the extraordinary bliss of Śakti— drink and experience wonder by means of the successive sequences of diverse opening and closing. Of what nature are you?

He stands in the middle, mounted upon Agni and Soma. For what purpose? It is for the sake of that which is deposited—that is, the projection—of the universe within the womb [of the Self], and for the sake of its manifestation in accordance with that [projection].
Of what nature are heaven and earth? They are asleep in the void, the subject of emptiness (*kha*), and this [universe] is awakened by *kalā*.
"Consciousness-essence consists of agency; for that which is insentient in nature, such as the Void (śūnya) and so forth, it exists as a limited quality.

According to this principle, with respect to those two who have submerged their ultimate essential nature by resorting to the state of the Void and Pradhāna and are standing face-to-face—how can they be said to be "asleep"?

"Facing each other in mutual rivalry as co-wives"— the meaning is that they have resorted to this confrontation because it is favorable to both. Even the external sun, by means of its nocturnal and lunar radiance, [illuminates] heaven and earth.

While the two [the sun and moon] are asleep—meaning their forms are closed—and are situated face-to-face, he, eager to taste their various essences (*rasa*), opens his lotus-like mouth with his rays and drinks up the terrestrial and atmospheric fluids.

This is for the sake of impregnation at the beginning of summer, so that they may enter within his own rays via the *karṣaṇī* and other channels; and at the beginning of the rainy season, it is for the sake of procreation.
From the emission of the first rays of the rain-cloud for the sowing of various medicinal herbs, and furthermore, while the two beloveds—

marked by the luster of the moon, smeared with camphor, and facing one another as they slept in rivalry— were lying there, the hero, situated between them, out of cleverness [fanned] their lotus-faces in turn with his breaths like cow-horns.

Having awakened her simultaneously and preceded by a kiss upon her eyes, he—being greedy for the nectar of the wine of her mouth—drinks it for the sake of pleasure, which serves as the cause for both the conception and the delivery of the embryo; thus, there is the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia), conjoined with the resonance (*dhvani*) of *śleṣa*. || 26 ||
Having prepared the *soma*— like a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) of full nectar— with his splendor, and having performed the *vaiśvadeva* rite that satisfies the world through the mouth of the fire,
he consumed the remnant of its digits in the sky like the *vighasa* of the new moon.
Like a householder within the cosmic egg, you perform the sacrifice of your own self. || 27 ||

O Sun! Having performed the sacrifice of your own self within the "house"—that is, in the midst of the four cosmic eggs (aṇḍas) consisting of Earth, Mūla-prakṛti, Māyā, and Śakti, which are characterized by the Śākta-Brahman situated in the *brahmarandhra*—what have you done? You have [offered] the Soma, which consists of fifteen aspects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, in this manner with your splendor (*tejas*).

Having prepared a sacrificial offering (*caru*) consisting of full nectar through the flashing of his own rays— considering that even within each single *tattva* there exists the nature of all thirty-six *tattvas*— and having established it as residing within himself, consisting of the manifestation of the universal self’s own Śākta nectar; [he is] one for whom the fire of *udāna* is the "fire" (*anala*), which is the means (*mukha*) for attaining [the goal].

Having performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice— which consists of the propitiation of that universe expanding as the path (adhvan) from Earth up to the Śiva-tattva, presided over by causes beginning with Brahmā and ending with Anāśrita— by means of that Soma and the sacrificial pap (caru), [he offers] the remainder of the portion of that Soma.

He eats, as if it were the *vighasa*— the remnant of the fifteen digits used for satiating the world— which consists of the digit called *amā*, belonging to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) known as the half-moment (*tuṭyardha*) remaining at the end, and which is like that which has swallowed all residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).
The nectar, in the form of the moon, is twofold and further sixteenfold;
all the gods drink its fifteen supreme digits.
She who dwells within the entire interior of the cave, she who is the new moon, and she who satisfies the universe.
Thus, according to the method taught in the *Śrīkālikākrama* and other texts, you are one who experiences the wonder of the universal deities within your own self as the ultimate reality.

What are you like? You are like a householder (*gṛhapati*). For he too, having prepared the sacrificial pap (*caru*) which is like full nectar on the new moon day, performs the *vaiśvadeva* rite—the satiation of the entire world headed by Agni—with that offering.

Consuming the remainder of that, he performs the sacrifice to his own self-deity. Even the external sun, having performed the satiation of the gods, sages, men, progenitors, and the world by means of the fifteen lunar digits (kalās) melted by the heat of its own rays, performs the sacrifice to the Self through the manifestation of the digit known as *amā*.
He ordains [all things] within the cosmic egg. || 27 ||
Having fashioned the unmanifest seed of the world like a day and night, within that very [seed], O Maker of Day, there is likewise another Brahma-period which is smaller than that;
and following in sequence, the periods of the gods, the ancestors, and humans are each progressively smaller.
By repeatedly performing [this], you cause the world to revolve through fivefold rotations. || 28 ||

O Sun of Consciousness, you who bring about the day that causes the arising of the universe; having made manifest— that is, having illuminated— that which is the seed of the entire world up to Sadāśiva, and which is the cause of its emergence and dissolution at its beginning and end,
consisting of time in the form of days and nights extending to the vast Parārdha as taught in the Śrī-Svacchanda and other scriptures.
In that very place [is] the seed of the internal world, consisting of the impure path from *kalā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*).

That is of the nature of *māyā* for a day and night; within that, too, is that which pertains to the unmanifest (*avyaktika*) and the primordial nature (*prākṛta*); within that, too, is that of Brahmā (*brāhma*); therein, too, is that of the gods (*daiva*); therein, too, is that of the ancestors (*pitrya*), relating to the fathers; and therein, too, is that of humans (*mānuṣa*).

Gradually making it smaller and smaller, as if acting through thousands of diversities and as if manifesting the entire universe, you fashion that which resides within and cast it outward by means of fivefold revolutions— the revolutions of the five diverse states beginning with waking; you create what is yet to be formed and you fashion what has already been created.

"You establish [objects] through the process of enumeration, thinking 'this is such-and-such, this is that'; even when established, you perceive them and withdraw them within; even when withdrawn, you perceive them and reflect upon them by purifying the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); even when reflected upon, you perceive them as non-different from your own self and bring them to the state of identity with your own self-luminous nature. And so it is once again."
From Your own nature, You manifest [the world] ever anew; You cause it to blossom.

Thus, You perform the play of mutual oscillation, encompassing the sports of creation, maintenance, dissolution, absorption into Your own self, and the manifestation of oneness with Yourself. Here, the seed-syllable of the universe (*jagadbīja*) should be repeated twice. The phrase "little by little" (*alpam alpaṃ*) expresses frequency (*vīpsā*).
This is the intended meaning: whatever [period] belongs to this [individual] for a day and night, that [is determined] either within his own movement of breath (*prāṇacāra*)—
even in its fractional parts—
or according to the procedure taught in the *Śrī-Svacchanda* and other texts, beginning with the rising of the months and ending with the rising of the sixty-year cycle.
In relation to the knowledge of the yogi, the Blessed One manifests [time] as extremely limited;
even there, because of the manifestation of the universal oneness within,
he manifests the entire calculation of time up to the end of the state of Sadāśiva— thus, this time which is being manifested is not [independent].
There is no real essence whatsoever in this [world]. For this very reason, the meaning is made clear by the word "as if" (*iva*) in the phrase "as if acting" (*kurvann iva*).

In reality, it shines forth that the Supreme Lord alone consists of the emergence, persistence, and dissolution of this entire universe; for there is nothing at all apart from Him whose sole body is consciousness. And here—
The measure of a human day and night and so forth is also stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda*:
"Likewise, thirty muhūrtas constitute a human day and night;
the southern solstice is the night, and the northern solstice is the day."
That [lunar month] is a day and night of the ancestors (pitaras); by this measure, a year is as previously described.
In the same way, a day and night of the gods (devas) [is calculated].
As for what has been stated here separately regarding the divine and the ancestral, that should be understood as the day and night pertaining to the ancestors.
For him, that [time] indeed takes the form of white and black. Furthermore:
A kalpa is declared to be a day of Brahmā, consisting of a thousand cycles of the four yugas;
thirty-six thousand such days constitute the dissolution and emergence of Brahmā.
"The day and night of the Rudras residing in the Unmanifest (avyakta) is equal to that [period];
by ten times the supreme age of Pradhāna (prādhānika-parārdha), Māyā withdraws everything and again creates the world. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
"This is proclaimed to be the day of the Lord Anāśrita, who is multiplied ten million times by the power of the final digit of time."

And so forth. Likewise, within a single movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*), beginning from the rising of one *ghaṭikā* up to the end of the rising of sixty years, everything is extensively detailed there;
however, for fear of excessive length, it has not been shown here. In this way, the Lord’s role as the transformer of the universe through the creation of day and night has been described. (28)
But those who are established in the tranquility of day and night are indeed supramundane; thus he says:
"Those who are fully awakened in the supreme light of reality on a sunlit day, or those who have entered the yogic sleep of the night of mental tranquility."
At the junctions of day and night, which are the supreme states of bliss, they pierce the solar light and proceed to the highest, most supreme light known as Nirvāṇa.

He is the heating one, whose nature is great light; those yogins who, by means of the method of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), have awakened— without the exertion of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the like— in the supreme light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), which is beautiful, eternally unclouded, never-setting, ultimate, permeating all states, and facing in every direction, through the light of reality (*tattvāloka*).

Those whose darkness of false cognition has dissolved; and others who, because the cessation of all external mental activity is the cause for the night that is the very tranquility of the mind, have entered the yogic sleep during that night;
those who have attained the unity of the tranquilized conceptualization and the manifestive consciousness—both of these [groups] as well.
At the very conclusion of the day and night as previously described, there are the Sandhyās, whose nature is supreme bliss;

they are the ground of the state of Śiva’s identity with the pervading Prāṇa and Apāna as they submerge. In them, having pierced the solar light—which is the supreme light of the vital breath, gross, and contracted illumination—[the yogi perceives] that which shines in all directions.
Having dissolved all conditioned phenomena, they always proceed upon the supreme path of Nirvāṇa and embrace the highest abode of Śakti. || 29 ||
You do not merely display a variegated reckoning of time and an absorption into a nature unreckoned by time;
you even manifest the arising and passing away of the entire world—thus he says:
"From Brahmā down to the end of all moving and stationary beings, this world appears as if new."
At every creation, O Sun, you emit [the world] with rays that swell the Soma;
and at the dissolution, you draw it back again through those same radiant beams.
Thus, at the beginning of each creation following its end, you display the play of your rays, manifesting your sovereign power according to the source from which they arose.
From the Śākta form up to that of Brahmā— excluding His own supreme Śākta form— this entire world, from Ādāśiva down to the earth, consisting of the two portions of mobile and immobile beings,
[arises] again and again in every creation, during the primal creation which consists of the unfolding of the Will.

With rays that are like cows— overflowing with soma and abounding in the nectar of Śakti— you emit [the world] and manifest your own form as rays that have become solidified. Then, by means of rays primarily consisting of blazing fire, you withdraw that universe back into its source at the time of dissolution, preceded by the re-entry of those respective causes manifested through your own sovereignty.

In the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), which consists of the manifestation of the identity with one's own consciousness, you draw back [the world] in reverse and make it consist solely of consciousness.
What are you doing? Manifesting the play of your rays—displaying the sport of your own beams—which possess manifest glory and clear majesty at the beginning and end of creation (*sarga*). || 30 ||

Having resorted to that form which is eternally accumulated and appropriate, the radiance of Brahman-splendor, and which exists among all beings through the process of creation, preservation, and dissolution—
he who is by nature invisible, like a great teacher among his disciples.
This very Self has been shown by you to the world through your own person as something directly perceptible.

O Blessed One, that Self which by its very nature and essence is beyond perception and outside the range of the senses, has been shown by you—among all beings in this world, among your disciples, and among those worthy of grace—to be directly perceived by yourself;
it has been made manifest through its own self-luminosity. Having done what? [Having abandoned] that which is eternally accumulated... always.

Having resorted to the form that is complete, appropriate, and a mass of consciousness-bliss, and having rendered oneself emerged by means of the submergence of the body and so forth—what kind of form? It is one whose manifestation is the light of Brahman-tejas; it is "Brahman" because of its vastness and its capacity to expand, and it is "tejas" (light) because it bestows non-duality; such is the light, such is the manifestation. By what kind [of means]?

By you— who are described as the source of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, who are devoid of birth and other such changes, and who, like a noble Guru who has perceived reality, reveals the Self to his disciples— your own Self is revealed; that is,
the consciousness-nature is made manifest within as the Supreme Self and externally as light in the form of the universe.
It is being made manifest. || 31 ||
All worlds are certainly situated within your body, and you, for the sake of the universe, simultaneously possess the qualities of each of them as if you were their possessor of attributes;
such being the case, O Blessed One, it is true that there is no one other than you who am I.
But you are the Knower and the Supreme Person, while I am by my very nature ignorant. || 32 ||

O Blessed One, whose form is embraced by Parāvāk— the nature of the power of absolute freedom (svātantryaśakti) and consisting of supreme bliss— within Your body, which is the cause of the universe and the cause of all things, and which is a mass of light and bliss, all the worlds [are contained].

The objects of perception and the perceivers—those subjects who are of the nature of Rudras and individual souls (kṣetrajñas)—are established. For how could these arise from you, the cause of the universe, without your existence which consists of consciousness?
And within each single body belonging to those worlds, you [exist] simultaneously and without succession.

[He] remains [thus]. Otherwise, how indeed could those [entities] shine without Your own luminosity? And therefore, although You are devoid of qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, You appear as if possessing qualities (*guṇin*) due to the quality of the manifestation of the nature of the universe. When the Self of the universe has been described in this way, [it is realized that] "I am the Truth, and there is no other"; however, You alone are such a supreme [Reality].

The *puruṣa* is the knowing subject, complete and possessing qualities such as omniscience. Yet, through you alone, he has been made to assume the state of a limited cognizer (*pramātṛ*) within the body and other such things; by nature, however, due to the majesty of your *māyā*, he is ignorant. Therefore, by submerging the state of being a cognizer in the body and so forth, and having stilled his ignorance through constant immersion in his own true self—
It is effectively stated that "cause my state of being known to emerge. || 32 ||

Through Your most excellent and ever-new grace, my entire range of faculties—will, desire, and so forth—along with my vital breath and speech, has become perfected; this birth of mine has become a place of refuge.
I consider that the duality of merit and demerit is now slowly seeking its end.
May devotion and faith toward your feet never be otherwise for me. || 33 ||

Thus, even for me who am ignorant, because of my devotion to you, and by virtue of the self-praise consisting of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that has proceeded toward the realization of the nature of consciousness (*cidātmatva*), there arises a *saṃkalpa*—
which is a gross desire— and a *icchā*, which is the cause of that *saṃkalpa*.
Its essence consists of the subtle reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) [of consciousness]. From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there are included:

effort (*prayatna*); immediately following that, all the organs of action (*karaṇa*)—with the exception of speech—engaged in perception, grasping, and other activities; and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which functions together with them. In all these cases, it is pervasive by virtue of being the nature of subtle reflective awareness.
The speech has remained thus, and these virtuous ones have become most excellent in my choosing and supreme favor;

likewise, this final birth has become a refuge—excellent for seeking shelter—and has resulted in being solely intent upon favoring those worthy of favor. For I, indeed, in all conditions, am devoted to the contemplation of the sun of consciousness while bestowing grace upon others.

He remained. Furthermore, I believe that through my own direct experience I perceive this: all that duality of merit and demerit, the collection of good and evil deeds accumulated over infinite births, remains as it slowly seeks its setting, dissolving like snow. For even when there is the destruction of all previously accumulated karma—
It is said that [the soul] "desires to go" because the karmas that initiate the body are on the verge of destruction. Regarding the phrase "otherwise":
if it were not so, how could devotion and faith toward your feet exist? They would certainly not exist.
As it is stated in the *Nandiśikhā*:
Whenever a longing for Śiva indeed arises in men constantly,
then those atoms arise possessing the conceit of being Śiva.
"At that very moment they are liberated; thereafter, they receive initiation from the Guru. Thus [it is said]. (33)

Truly, for those who have taken refuge in you, there are no further births or deaths; even among these, I pray for this one fruit of praising you: that you, the Lord of the three worlds, like supreme tranquility itself, may be born of me—though you are of a meritorious body and yet unborn.
May I remain steadfast like a boat in the ocean of saṃsāra for the sake of ferrying the world across. || 34 ||
O Lord, although for those who have taken refuge in You and are pervaded by You,
there is no further birth or death due to the burning away of all latent impressions that cause saṃsāra,
nevertheless, I beg for this one final birth, which has as its sole fruit Your praise and Your hymn of glory. Just as:

This [state] bestows the wonder of the self-awareness that consumes worldly existence; therefore, by this very means—being permeated by the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of praise for You—the supreme state of peace (*paraḥ śamaḥ*) is attained even in this very body.
According to the etymological derivation that "the universe is stilled (*śāmyati*) within this," it is like the supreme nature of Śaṅkara (Śiva) within the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

The Lord is the master of the three worlds, and not dependent on others. For this very reason, may I be one whose body is meritorious—that is, one who bestows grace upon others through sight, touch, and so forth; and being "not born of a womb" (ayoni), a single solid mass of eternally manifest consciousness and bliss, may I remain steady like a raft or a ship in the midst of the ocean of saṃsāra for the sake of delivering the entire universe.
May I exist for a long time. || 34 ||
Having entered through the path of nectar via the Suṣumṇā, you first nourish the gods, humans, and ancestors with your cool-rayed nature and your peaceful digits;
afterwards, you enter the waters and various medicinal herbs, even while remaining within them.
Thus you gladden the three worlds; therefore, O Sun, you are the friend of the universe.
O Arka! For this reason, you possess friendship toward the world, which is denoted by the etymological term *mitra* (friend);

for, having attained the state of the cool-rayed one—the nature of the moon—as the apāna-moon by means of the nourishing central path of the *sauṣumṇa*, you first reach all [the deities], beginning with the gods.
"You nourish the subjects" means you cause them to attain their established state. By what?

By the "peaceful" powers (*kalās*), which have withdrawn external manifestation through inward-turnedness and consist of the inherent power of self-reflection from the initial emission (*visarga*) to its end. Immediately thereafter is "water" (*ambhas*).
You enter all the currents that have begun to flow outward and make them drenched in Your own nectar;

You enter the various medicinal herbs and render all external appearances, such as stationary objects and the like, filled with Your own self-luminosity. Thus, although You manifest within that [world] as the nature of the manifold of objects of knowledge, the entire threefold universe is thus [of Your essence].

By the very method of reflecting upon that manifestation, having attained the state of the moon, you satisfy and nourish the gods and others according to the principle previously stated. Even the external sun, by the method of transferring nectar through the path of the *suṣumṇā*,
attains the state of the moon and nourishes the gods and others according to the aforementioned principle, with its peaceful rays— that is, with its ceased brilliance.
Through its digits (kalās) or powers (śaktis), the Sun enters the waters during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) and assumes the form of rain;

it enters the plants and makes them succulent. Moving therein, by means of the sequence of primary and secondary Vaiśvadeva sacrifices, it nourishes the three worlds and thus demonstrates its very nature as a friend to the universe. || 35 ||
O Lord, while darkness still persists,

this mind of mine, though not yet withdrawn within, does not abandon its deep sleep at the end of the night; therefore, like a lotus-pond by the light of its own radiance, may it be awakened by you who have dispelled all gloom.
This [energy] belongs to the Sun; O Maker of Day, let it be quickly led to supreme awakening. (36)

O Lord, O Sun, O Master, O Solar Consciousness, when you have sniffed at the darkness of ignorance— having it trampled underfoot so that it is utterly eradicated— then this intellect of mine, though the end of attachment and aversion has occurred and though it is inward-turned and deeply absorbed within, does not [awaken from] its profound sleep regarding the manifestation of non-difference from You.

He abandons it. Therefore, by means of that self-luminous radiance (*ātmabhāsā*)—which is your own light and serves as the cause—you, by which darkness has been made to set, should very quickly lead [this consciousness] to the supreme awakening, the state of being the self whose nature is the light of one's own realization known as "tranquility" (*praśānta-akhyāti*). The Sun is the deity.

Considering her to be "saurī" (belonging to the sun), she is like a *padminī* or *nalinī* (a lotus plant). She too, at the end of the night (*doṣāvasāne*)—that is, at dawn—when the darkness has been overcome, does not abandon her deep sleep with her petals closely clinging to the pericarp; rather, she is awakened by his own light, which dispels the darkness and intensifies the radiance.
By you. || 36 ||
O Lord, having brought to its end that darkness by which the entire world seemed as if swallowed up, and with Your heart again perfumed by compassion,
You maintain the two courses— white and black— dividing them for both night and day.
Therefore, O Bhānu, you are my protector even from this evil deed that brings about my defeat in existence.

O All-pervading Lord, Sun, garlanded with rays of pure consciousness, you who have withdrawn and destroyed that darkness of ignorance by which this world was swallowed up— having done so out of compassion for those favored by you, as if your heart were touched by mercy, you divide the white and black paths at the time of emergence.

Having descended from the plane of inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇāpāna*), you again sustain—that is, nourish—that darkness; the meaning is that you do not instantly bestow the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) from which there is no emergence. Just as the external sun, having destroyed the darkness that had swallowed the world, [returns] by day and night as if out of compassion, during the night and the day.

"Because you divide [the light], you bear it, and you nourish it"—this is a *śleṣopamā* (pun-based simile). Since you thus possess compassion even for the evil-minded darkness (*tamas*), therefore, even in my humiliation—that is, in the affliction (*kleśa*) consisting of rising up [in anger]—be my protector and savior. Of what kind of humiliation? Of "badly done," meaning an evil action.
The meaning is: "Make me one who tastes the flavor of the immersion that is beyond emergence, wherein there is no humiliation regarding the rejection or acceptance of sense objects. || 37 ||

Having emerged from meditation and not yet attained immersion (*samāveśa*), intent on censuring the state of emergence, he spoke to the Blessed One, who is devoted to immersion, in order to pray [to him]:
"Of those who rely on the bonds of good and evil karma accumulated since beginningless saṃsāra..."
O Lord, for us who are afflicted by old age, disease, birth, death, hunger, and thirst,
and who have been blinded by the powerful darkness of false knowledge— wherever we may dwell— be our protector through your compassion. (38)

"Good merit" (sat-puṇya) and "bad sin" (asat-pāpa); "of those situated here or there" means in whatever place, time, or variety of condition they may be, he is the "protector" (trātā), that is, the guardian through the manifestation of his immersion [in consciousness]. The remainder is clear. || 38 ||
Of those whose speech falters between truth and falsehood, who are devoid of purity and shame, who are ignorant, who are distressed by prayers for both fruit and its absence,
and who harbor curiosity for all objects in every state—
Be our protector as a father for us children who are greedy for enjoyments. || 39 ||

"Be our protector as a father—that is, as a progenitor—unto us who are like children and fools, greedy for enjoyments and the pleasures of the senses," as stated previously. For you are indeed our progenitor from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*); this is the same whether [the relationship] be considered real or unreal. In one case, there is a lapse or error (*skhalita*).

Elsewhere, there is indistinctness of syllables. Likewise, purity is both mental and physical. That which is fruitless or fruitful prayer belongs to those who are cowardly and lacking in fortitude. As for the phrase "of those who pray for that," the rest is easily understood. || 39 ||
Old age wastes away the body as long as death has not arrived with its messenger;
nor does that terrible noose, shaped like a three-hooded serpent and difficult to resist,
suddenly and firmly seize the throat while licking up one's life.
O giver of fearlessness to your devotees, be gracious for our ultimate welfare. || 40 ||

O Giver of Fearlessness to devotees, as long as we do not encounter the miserable state ending with death and its subsequent emergence [into rebirth], be gracious to us and become purified by the pacification of the impurities of the latent impressions (saṃskāras) of the body and so forth. [Grant] the supreme immersion, which is a dense mass of light and bliss, free from all emergence.
The meaning is: "Make us happy by tasting the nectar of death. The rest is clear. || 40 ||

As long as this body, having seen the mouth of Death— fierce with the arrogance of its play of licking the breath of all living beings, terrifying with its burning eyes and formidable fangs— does not flee in fear toward the five elements (death), [so long must one practice].
O Sun, consisting of eternal nectar, protect us who are fleeing in all directions. 41.

O Sun of Consciousness (cidarka), consisting of eternal nectar, whose very nature is a single mass of unceasing supreme bliss— before this body, composed of the eight constituents (sapuryaṣṭaka), sees the mouth of Death, the Ender, and out of sheer terror does not succumb to the fivefold dissolution (pañcatā), protect us who are bewildered during the state of emergence (vyutthāna).

Protect us who cry out, "Which direction is ours? Which direction is this?"—for what direction can there be for one who has not attained immersion (*samāveśa*) in You? Grant us that immersion from which there is no emergence. What is the mouth of Death like?
It is a swelling tongue that devours life and swallows the vital breaths of all beings, characterized by the restless movement of its flickering tongue.
In such a rage, he was bold and arrogant; likewise, his eyes were burning and scorching; and likewise, he was formidable with his fierce and powerful fangs. 41.
Your body, which is the abode of the Yajus and Sāman, has the form of sound like the sky;
its seven horses are the seven meters, and its chariot-fender is composed of the Ṛgveda.
Thus, because you consist of all the Vedas, or rather, through the grace of my compassion—
Quickly hear from me this piteous and compassionate cry.
O Blessed One, by Your definitive vision, You are one whose abode and splendor consist of the Sāmaveda; whose body and form consist of the Yajurveda, pervasive like the ether;
and who, being the substratum of all sounds, manifests those very sounds—indeed, even the Gāyatrī and other [Vedic meters].

Your horses are the seven meters; the mandala, the radiance, and even the halo are composed of the Ṛgveda—thus, because you consist of all the Vedas. Alternatively, out of compassion (anukampā) and grace (anugraha), from me—that is, from my presence—because of your devotion to the prayers spoken and yet to be spoken, [you appear] piteous and dispirited.

And because it reveals the nature of saṃsāra, listen— immediately upon its utterance— with compassion and a desire to favor us, to this lamentation which is permeated by the essence of pity and intent upon praying for your grace. || 42 ||
Thinking that those who have taken refuge at my feet do not meet destruction even when being swallowed by the gods, the Moon— displaying his own fame as if it were white throughout the three worlds—
I believe, O Vivasvat, has his body diminished through growth within my womb.
You gradually lead your own white radiance through the *suṣumṇā* by means of its luminous rays.

O Blessed One, O Vivasvān, O Sun of Consciousness! Even when seized by the gods, those who have taken refuge at our feet do not meet destruction; thus, as if displaying a white and radiant fame throughout the three worlds, [the rays of the sun] fall upon the moon—which has its body diminished, whose digits are entirely swallowed even by the gods, and which is like the light of the central channel known as Suṣumṇā.

I believe— that is, I know— that by means of those rays, which are light acting as the cause, and through the increase within the womb of the digit called *amā*, you lead your own white shadow— that is, your fully bright luster— to its completion. Here, from the perspective of the secret doctrine, the gods are the sense organs (*indriyas*).
The Moon, having entered within through the yoga of the downward breath (apāna), consists of the sixteen digits as its nature; this entire range of objects of knowledge (meyavarga),
its digits being diminished through the swallowing of those digits by means of the yoga of the radiance of all-outflows, becomes the New Moon (amā) through the splendor of the rays of the Suṣumṇā—
the expansion of the central abode— and through the light of the manifestation of the Fourth State (turya), known as "Auspicious" (śubha).

The meaning is: within the womb of the power (*śakti*) vibrating for half a moment (*tuṭyardha*), there is an internal growth that has been made to throb by the flashes of the potency of Śakti (*śāktavīryabhābhiḥ*), which manifest and subside through the predominance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other factors; by means of that [growth], you lead—that is, you cause one to reach—the white [state] which is a single mass of consciousness (*cidekaghana*). The external [explanation], however, is clear. || 43 ||
Let alone your service from the time of birth; for who in this world can describe that which yields immeasurable fruit through the means of both worldly enjoyment and liberation?
Even at the end of life, may that radiant light alone remain within the path of my memory.
Since you are capable of leading the virtuous to nirvāṇa, who else could be equal to you? 44.

O Radiant One, that service rendered to you from birth onwards yields immeasurable fruit; by whom can it be described, or by whom is it possible to speak of it, since it cannot be delimited by any measure? This is because it takes the form of both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*); for enjoyment, which is the very experience of sense objects, grants repose in the bliss of one's own Self.

Liberation is indeed the manifestation of one's own nature as the living Śiva, and enjoyment is the state of being immersed in the wonder of consciousness, not attachment to sense objects. You, whose essence is pure light, reveal that enjoyment and liberation to your devotees who have become absorbed in you, and even at the moment of death when final extinction occurs, you manifest for the virtuous.
Having entered the path of mindfulness, you are capable of leading to nirvāṇa and liberation; therefore, who else is equal to you? The meaning is that your majesty is extraordinary. || 44 ||
For men, that fruit which is indirect— such as worshiping the gods who are beyond direct perception— is indeed consistent with its cause, for the effect must correspond to the cause.
But since you are directly perceptible to all the worlds, this fruit of mine is manifest before my very eyes.
Therefore, I request that which is appropriate for your devotion, just as [I have requested] you. 45.

It is logical that for those who worship deities such as Indra and Candra—who are not perceptible—the fruit consisting of the attainment of heaven and so forth is imperceptible and occurs at a later time; for everywhere, an effect is consistent with its cause, just as a clay pot is made from clay. But you are the sun of consciousness.

It is directly perceptible to all as self-luminous, for nothing whatsoever shines without the self-luminosity of the sun of consciousness (*cidarka*). Therefore, by reason of my devotion to You, the appropriate fruit—which consists of immersion (*samāveśa*) into You who are eternally risen—is rightly mine. For this reason, I ask for and pray for that fruit; just as when there are deities who possess agency (*kṛtimatī*).
I entreat you alone; likewise, I entreat for that very fruit which consists of the state of absorption from which there is no emergence, and not some limited thing at all. 45.
And those who say that even when served, the Blessed One bestows only health— those are knowers of reality, fortunate ones in this world who are preeminent in the attainment of enjoyments;
for they possess that which is the fullness of all joys for the worlds, both in worldly enjoyment and in liberation.
For who indeed could be the giver of another body made of nectar to him? || 46 ||

Furthermore, those who, though their primary fruit—the immersion into the Self—is not yet discerned, say that "the Lord, when served, bestows health," they too are knowers of reality and fortunate in this world;
for, being primarily intent on enjoyment and yoga, they desire health for the sake of both enjoyment and yoga. And this is indeed logical.

For what else indeed—other than the sun of consciousness (*cidarka*), whose body is nectar, who is a dense mass of the radiance of supreme bliss, and who is the self of perfect happiness—could be the giver of enjoyment and liberation, as well as the support for those two and of health? None at all.

This is because of the prohibitive rule regarding the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with words meaning "satisfaction" (*tṛpti*), based on the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārtha* (Pāṇini 2.2.11).
In the phrase "full of pleasures," the genitive case is used [to express the relationship]. || 46 ||
Having repeatedly abandoned even their various heavy fickle natures for my sake, as if they had been made to share a single purpose through their service to you;
I desire to repay the favor of those beloved senses of mine.
Therefore, O Lord of the Day, grant me at the outset this favor toward them.

O Lord of Days, O Sun of Consciousness, by means of those senses—the internal and external organs—having abandoned and cast aside great restlessness, profound instability that recurs again and again, as well as various personal objects consisting of repose in sense-objects and manifold individual purposes; [...he remains...
