Through the method of turning inward by serving You, my cultivation of You has been made one with my beloved alone and embraced with resolute intent. I desire to bring benefit to those beloved ones, my own senses; therefore, first grant me grace toward them.
The meaning is: by abandoning the illusory body, manifest your own nature as the circle of rays. || 47 ||
What name is uttered such that you are not its utterer?
What is that which is expressed by all speech, O Universal Form, which you are not? Therefore, whatever is spoken—even that—in praise of you, arises from the yoga of devotion.
O Blessed One, by your grace, may this become auspicious for us. 48.

O You of universal form, O Unconditioned One, whatever we have uttered out of devotion to You regarding the subject of Your praise— being for the most part inconsistent due to our preoccupation with the limitation of "this-ness" (idantā)— may that become blessed through Your grace, by which the internal purity of the universe, consisting of both the signified and the signifier, is attained.
May it manifest as nothing other than Your own form. || 48 ||

That which points out the path of the gods beginning with the cool season (śiśira) and the north, or that which points out the dark path of the ancestors (pitṛpatha) and the south beginning with the rainy season (prāvṛṭ); other than these two is the intermediate one, situated between the equinox (viṣuvat) and the zenith (abhijit), devoid of ritual action (kṛtya).
May my state be that of some fortunate woman who exists as an intermediary between Prakṛti and Puruṣa. || 49 ||

May my disposition and state of being—certainly extraordinary, blessed, and consisting of spiritual attainment—abide between the two, in the midst of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, who are the left and right arms [respectively]. Of what nature is it? It is *viṣuvat*, because it is worthy (*arhati*) of pervasion (*viṣu*); it is *abhijit*, because it prevails (*abhijayati*), existing with supreme excellence through the pacification of duality.

It is called *madhyamā* because it abides in the center of all. It is empty of activities such as the gentle or the cruel, because its essence is rest in one’s own bliss (*svānanda*). Likewise, it is the *devayāna* (the path of the gods) because it causes delight to the deity; it consists of a radiance that extends from the heart up to the *dvādaśānta*.

The upward path, the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), which possesses the nature of the cold season, spring, and summer, is that function called *prāṇa* which directs and expands [the breath]; or else, the downward path, the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), which consists of the rainy season, autumn, and winter, is that function called *apāna* whose form is the entry into the heart from the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*).
Because it bestows enjoyment (*bhoga*), it is *kṛṣṇa*; because it is the cause of the ancestors' satisfaction, it points out the path of the ancestors (*pitṛpatha*).
Other than these two, there is another which bestows liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); this is the meaning of the term *unmanā*.

The meaning is that the rising of the zodiac signs, beginning with Capricorn (*makara*), occurs at intervals of six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) starting from the heart within the thirty-six finger-breadths of the body.
It exists in the Śrīsvacchanda and other such scriptures. || 49 ||
Having remained for a while as if drinking with the mind alone in the midst of the bridge,
and having reached the goal— the firm state— and then having clearly torn away the palate,
one reaches a certain supreme void above the Truth (Satya), which is devoid of moon and fire.
Having become one with Brahman, may I go to you, situated between the paths of the gods and the ancestors.
Between the two paths of the gods and the ancestors—

having determined for myself the upward and downward courses of the way of the gods and the way of the ancestors— and by virtue of the word "and" (ca), having attained uninterruptedness as one who has become Brahman within all flowing streams, may I go unto you.

May I become the form of the sun of consciousness, which is the supreme reality of the Self. Of what nature are You? You are that indescribable, supreme void—the sky of unsurpassed consciousness—which is above the abode of equanimity (sāmarasya) that bestows existence upon the universe through Truth; which is a single mass of light and bliss; and which is free from moon, fire, and the void (somāgniśūnya).

The refinement of the prāṇa and apāna breaths becomes completely stilled. Having done what? Having brought about the manifestation of the abode of the fierce knot known as the palate and the lambikā; having torn it away and pierced through by means of the support of the divine binding of the senses. Then, immediately thereafter, having attained the fixed state (dhruvapada).
Having reached the station of *bindu*, which consists of the light that differentiates all objects of knowledge, [the yogi] stands in the middle of the bridge-dam; there,
by means of the upward power (*ūrdhva-śakti*) that effects obstruction,
the creation consisting of the *nāda*— which is the means for crossing over the prāṇa, apāna, and so forth flowing between the two banks— is restrained.

Standing at the gateway of all the apertures and ascending slightly, as it were, drinking in [the breath], he pacifies the mental impressions associated with the conceptualizing mind up to the level of *samanā*. || 50 ||
He who, through speech, mind, body, and intellect, desires to ascend to the very yoga of equanimity and the subsiding of passion and hatred— the sun’s state of being the self of all—
and seeks liberation from the tether that swallows both merit and demerit, [should employ] this reasoning-conjoined [method].
Thus did that illustrious Sāmba offer this hymn of praise to Ravi, which was composed in his own tranquil style. || 51 ||

"Yogins take refuge in her"—thus [he called her] Śrī; together with that Fortune, which is the Goddess of Liberation (mokṣalakṣmī), Sāmba—the son of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—composed this hymn to Ravi, the Sun of Consciousness, characterized by such [qualities]. Alternatively, there is the reading "supratiṣṭhām" (well-established).

What kind of praise? One joined with reasoning (*yukti*), which consists of the yoga of resting in the supreme nature; that is to say, one that makes that [nature] manifest. He shows the referent of the word "that" (*sa*):
those [praises] which concern the universal selfhood—that is, the omniformity—of the Sun, the cause of all, who is the light of consciousness.

He desires *yoga*, which is oneness (*ekatva*), according to the perspective of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). According to the perspective stated as "the union with another reality," he wishes to ascend—that is, he desires to appropriate—*yoga* as supreme identity (*paraikya*), and nothing else. What kind of *yoga*? It is that equanimity (*samatā*) or equality (*sāmya*) which arises when attachment and aversion—the two foremost of all defects—are pacified.
Of what nature is that? By what means? By the intellect accompanied by speech, mind, and body. By speech, through hymns of praise;

by the mind, through continuous reflection (*anusaṃdhāna*); by the body, through prostration consisting of immersion, primarily by means of bodily contact; and by the intellect, through determination (*adhyavasāya*). For what purpose is this [offering]?
He says that he offered praise as follows: "The very act of devouring the world—which, by implication, is unawakened—by means of dharma and adharma is itself the *raśanā*, the binding rope;
for the sake of liberation from that [rope], people may attain liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) through the recitation and contemplation of this hymn. This is the intended meaning.
This hymn, both manifest and profound, containing the essence of the supreme self, was spoken by Śrī Sāmba— the beloved of all young women such as devotion and faith.
He who recites this Sāvitra hymn regularly [elevates] all worlds like his own self.
Beholding it at the end, he goes to the orb of the sun, just like Śuka. || 52 ||

This hymn, which contains the inner essence (*adhyātmagarbha*) and embraces the secret (*kroḍīkṛtarahasya*), is manifest through the perception of external objects yet profound due to its connection with the internal meaning; this *sāvitra* hymn, related to the sun of consciousness (*cidbhānu*), was spoken by Śrī Sāmba for anyone who [offers it] to all worlds as if to his own self.

Perceiving the entire universe as non-different from the self of consciousness, and contemplating it with certainty for the sake of praise, he recites it constantly and reflects upon it incessantly; at the end, he enters the orb of the fierce-rayed sun of consciousness—which devours duality—a wheel of rays in which the entire universe has been dissolved and attained a state of equal flavor. He becomes identical with that, like a parrot.

Like the son of the blessed Vyāsa. Of what sort was Sāmba? He was the beloved, by whom not even for a moment could he be forsaken, of all those young and ever-new beauties—namely, those whose primary qualities were devotion and faith, and who were characterized by reflections on the meaning of reality and so forth. But not...

By this [statement], which conveys a meaning obtainable through contrast—that he is desirable to all external women solely by virtue of his preeminent beauty and charm—he reveals his own status as the son of the Blessed Vāsudeva. || 52 ||
Desiring to favor people through this manner of conclusion, he offers this benediction:
"Thus ends this fifty-verse hymn on the supreme secret, a discourse on Brahman according to the Āgamas, which possesses the fresh merit of the sun."
May she, when described and heard by you, remove our misfortune and grant the attainment of auspiciousness to those who possess devotion toward her as toward a mother. 53.

Thus, according to the sequence stated, this fifty-verse hymn of praise to the Blessed One, the Sun of Consciousness (*cidarka*), whose majesty is wonderfully diverse in the universe and remains unbroken— composed of verses ending with "staying as if drinking a little like the mind," endowed with the meaning of the great secret— is meritorious and purifying. Likewise, it is accompanied by the scriptures (*sāgamā*).

May this discourse on Brahman, as described by us— which embodies the true essence of the meaning of the scriptures of Maheśvara, whose nature is the Upaniṣads of the universe, and which consists of the supreme non-dual contemplation— having been heard by you all, may it remove misfortune, destroy sin, and eliminate evil intentions.
May he grant the auspicious accomplishment to those who possess devotion, and may he bring about the desired glory of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; may there be auspiciousness! 53.
A certain Śaiva, Kṣemarāja— who possesses the helplessness born of the intense surge of a fresh state of immersion, characterized by a profound passion for absorption into Paraśiva—
has undertaken the composition of this commentary on this excellent hymn.
This is not so; for the virtuous must demonstrate what has been established with immediate clarity.

Thus concludes the *Śrīsāmbapañcāśikā*, together with the commentary composed by Rājānaka Śrī Kṣemarāja, who lives in dependence upon the lotus feet of the venerable Abhinavagupta, the most excellent teacher of the Great Maheśvara.
It is finished.
This treatise is completed.
